paper_title: Intern-Decision: Efficient Multimodal Decision Making with Autoregressive Masked Language Modeling

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Interactive agents repeatedly choose among a finite set of actions, labels, or ordinal outcomes. Generating a free-form response for each choice adds latency and complicates the interface between a model and its environment. We present Intern-Decision, a family of 0.8B, 2B, and 4B multimodal decision models that return structured choices and candidate probabilities from text and optional images. Our autoregressive masked language modeling objective places one decision placeholder per field in a complete assistant JSON skeleton. Ground-truth symbols appear only in supervision, while all fields are evaluated in a single causal forward pass using the backbone's native language-model head. The 4B model achieves a 90.02% unweighted average accuracy across seven evaluation suites, compared with 88.74% for Jev v1.13.0. For a fixed 289-token request with three fields on one RTX 4090, mean latency is 44.16 ms for the 4B model and approximately 33--34 ms for the smaller models. On a separate 96-case known-distribution pilot, temperature scaling reduces expected multiclass Brier from 0.628 to 0.550 and expected calibration error from 0.213 to 0.089. A confidence-based handoff study on 111 public Jevbench-Hard items improves accuracy from 82/111 (73.87%) to 97/111 (87.39%) by routing 42 items to Atria-Dawn-Preview. We also describe qualitative game, visual interface, and browser demonstrations. These results support compact decision models as a practical component of larger agent systems.

Code: https://github.com/InternLM/Intern-Decision Models: https://huggingface.co/collections/internlm/intern-decision 1. Introduction Driven by the rapid progress of large language models (LLMs), agent systems have evolved from passive text generation models into interactive systems capable of perceiving environments, using tools, and taking actions [19, 30, 32]. Unlike open-ended text generation, many agent operations are inherently closed-set decision problems, where the model selects from predefined set of alternatives, such as tool invocation, model routing, and actions [20]. However, current agents often rely on autoregressive free-form generation even when the underlying task only requires structured decisions, introducing additional decoding overhead and complicating the interface between models and downstream controllers [19, 25, 30]. These observations motivate the development of dedicated decision models that can directly produce structured outcomes together with reliable confidence estimates for efficient agent execution. Recent work on structured decision models, referred to as System-1 decision models, explores this perspective by replacing unrestricted generation with explicit decision interfaces and probabilistic outputs. Systems such as Jev [27] provide typed interfaces for choice, score, and binary decisions, while several open implementations investigate alternative architectures and inference strategies for efficient structured decision making [1, 17, 22, 26]. These interfaces primarily target textual decisions, and implementations differ in whether they score multiple questions jointly or separately. For multimodal agents operating in dynamic environments, decision Intern-Decision: Efficient Multimodal Decision Model models must additionally integrate visual observations, task instructions, and changing interface states, where action selection depends jointly on visual evidence and contextual constraints [28, 29]. Moreover, practical agent requests often require multiple decisions over shared state, creating need for efficient multi-field decision models that can preserve the capabilities of pretrained multimodal language models while providing structured outputs. To address these challenges, we introduce Intern-Decision, family of multimodal decision models based on autoregressive masked language modeling. Our approach reformulates structured decision making as next-token prediction over masked decision fields within predefined assistant output schema. By retaining the pretrained causal language model backbone and native language-model head, Intern-Decision evaluates multiple candidate decisions in single forward pass and produces both structured predictions and candidate probabilities without iterative text generation. This design separates decision scoring from free-form response decoding, enabling efficient inference while preserving compatibility with existing multimodal language models. To adapt pretrained models to this decision-oriented interface, we construct unified multimodal decision corpus consisting of textual states, optional images, typed questions, and target decisions. The corpus combines teacher-constructed challenging decisions with public task distributions, covering textual reasoning, instructionfollowing decisions, visual judgments, interface actions, and interactive control scenarios. We instantiate Intern-Decision with 0.8B, 2B, and 4B Qwen3.5 backbones [23], fine-tuning the language backbone while keeping the vision tower and projector frozen. To improve the reliability of confidence estimates, we further apply post-hoc temperature scaling [13] using separate calibration split. We evaluate Intern-Decision from three perspectives: decision accuracy, inference efficiency, and probability quality. Across seven evaluation suites, including public Jevbench subsets [10], Intern-Decision-4B achieves 90.02% unweighted mean accuracy, compared with 88.74% for Jev. For fixed 289-token request containing three decision fields, Intern-Decision-4B achieves mean latency of 44.16 ms on single RTX 4090. We further evaluate probability calibration through separate known-distribution pilot and study confidence-based model routing, in which requests are passed to larger model when the decision models confidence falls below threshold. Qualitative demonstrations on visual interaction and browser assistance further illustrate how compact decision models can serve as local decision modules within hierarchical agent systems. Our contributions are summarized as follows: We introduce Intern-Decision, family of compact multimodal decision models that formulate structured decision making as next-token-aligned masked prediction, enabling multi-field candidate scoring with native language-model head in single causal forward pass. We develop unified multimodal decision framework, evaluate accuracy, latency, and calibration under separate protocols, and illustrate visual interaction through qualitative demonstrations. We investigate confidence-based model handoff that passes low-confidence requests to larger model, and demonstrate how compact structured decision models can complement larger models in interactive agent systems. 2. Related Work Decision Models. Recent decision models target fast, structured judgments: given state, questions, and predefined answer options, they return typed decisions with probability estimates rather than free-form text. Alongside TypeSafes Jev [27], which supports choice, score, and binary decisions and reports using Reinforcement Learning for Calibrated Decisions (RLCD), related open implementations explore different modeling and inference strategies for structured decision-making. JevK5 [1] adapts Qwen3.5 with LoRA and derives candidate probabilities from next-token logits through Jev-style interface. Kev [17] combines Qwen backbones with LoRA adapters and learned pointer head, providing self-hostable models and an API for typed choices and scores. SemIf-OpenJev [26] provides direct-scoring approach that derives option probabilities from candidate-token logits of frozen language models, with optional shared-state prefill reuse across questions. Laya [22] adopts an encoder-based, non-autoregressive architecture to produce choice, score, and yes/no decisions in single forward pass. Within this paradigm, Intern-Decision focuses on multimodal structured decision-making, incorporating visual inputs alongside textual states and task instructions. Intern-Decision: Efficient Multimodal Decision Model Autoregressive and Masked Prediction. Autoregressive language models such as GPT-3 [5] predict tokens conditioned on causal prefix, whereas BERT [8] reconstructs masked tokens using bidirectional context. Hybrid approaches explore combinations of these paradigms: UniLMv2 [3] combines autoencoding and partially autoregressive objectives through pseudo masking, while GLM [9] combines bidirectional encoding of the corrupted input with autoregressive reconstruction of masked spans. Mask-Predict [12] predicts masked target tokens in parallel and iteratively refines uncertain predictions. For classification, PET [24] uses patternverbalizer pairs for cloze-based prediction and distills the resulting models into sequence classifier, while LM-BFF [11] performs prompt-based fine-tuning with label words and demonstrations, reusing the pretrained masked-language-model head. Intern-Decision formulates structured decisions as autoregressive masked language modeling, combining answer placeholders with next-token-aligned prediction in causal multimodal model. Its native language-model head scores candidates for all requested fields in single forward pass, without iterative refinement or answer feedback. Calibration and selective computation. Temperature scaling fits positive scalar to adjust predictive confidence while preserving the most likely label [13]. Brier scoring evaluates the full predictive distribution [4], complementing accuracy and binned calibration error. Confidence-based routing and cascading use uncertainty to allocate requests between models with different costs [6, 7]. Our evaluation separates hard-label calibration from an exact-distribution pilot and reports one escalation operating point rather than an optimized routing policy. 3. Autoregressive Masked Decision Modeling 3.1. Problem formulation Let 𝑥 = (𝑠, 𝐼, 𝑄) denote request with state 𝑠, optional ordered images 𝐼, and ordered questions 𝑄 = (𝑞1, . . . , 𝑞𝑚). Question 𝑞𝑗 has field identifier, an instruction, and an ordered candidate set 𝒞𝑗. The model returns categorical distribution 𝑃𝑗 and selected label ˆ𝑦𝑗 𝒞𝑗 for every field. The supported types are choice, noul, and score. Choice labels follow the insertion order of their criteria; Boolean labels are ordered as no, yes; ordinal labels are strings such as 0, 1, and 2. deterministic mapping 𝑎𝑗 : 𝒞𝑗 𝒱 assigns each option legal single-token answer symbol from the tokenizer vocabulary 𝒱. The release supports 62 candidate symbols; the HTTP service permits up to 16 fields per request. These are interface limits rather than claims about generalization to arbitrarily large schemas. Field and option order remain unchanged during compilation and scoring. 3.2. Input construction and causal readout The released compiler places the state and ordered decision schema in the user turn, then appends an assistant JSON skeleton with one reserved <decision> token per field. Figure 1 presents readable view of constructed support-ticket request with choice, score, and noul fields. Choice symbols follow criteria order, score symbols follow list order from 0, and Boolean symbols are for no and for yes. The target panel shows the mapped answer symbols A, C, and B, corresponding to billing, urgency 2, and yes. Training supervises these symbol tokens at the decision positions; inference maps predicted symbols back to the original labels. The displayed JSON groups the supervision targets for illustration and is not inserted into the input or supervised as complete generated JSON response. Labels, reference distributions, benchmark rationales, and provenance are excluded from the visible evidence. Training and inference use the same masked skeleton, and changing target must not change the input token sequence. Let 𝑝𝑗 be the token position of the placeholder for field 𝑗. causal backbone computes hidden states ℎ1, . . . , ℎ𝐿, and the native LM head produces vocabulary logits 𝑧𝑡. The released objective reads the position immediately before the marker: (1) The answer label is stored at position 𝑝𝑗 in the supervision tensor, so the ordinary causal shift pairs it with 𝑧𝑝𝑗 1. No ground-truth answer symbol is inserted into the input. Earlier placeholders are visible to later fields 𝑧𝑝𝑗 1 = LMHead(ℎ𝑝𝑗 1). 3 Intern-Decision: Efficient Multimodal Decision Model Shared state Customer message: bought headphones yesterday and noticed today that was charged twice. Please refund the extra charge as soon as possible. Blue panels show visible evidence and masked assistant context; gold shows target answer symbols: for billing, for urgency 2, and for yes. These symbols supervise the decision positions and never enter the input. System instructions, control tokens, and some option descriptions are omitted or shortened. through causal attention, but their gold or predicted answers are not fed back. All requested logits are collected from the same forward pass. All fields share the same state and schema, and their placeholders are processed together. The readout uses next-token alignment, not same-position supervision. 3.3. Training objective For batch with 𝑀 supervised fields, the loss is full-vocabulary cross-entropy at the shifted decision positions: ℒdecision = 1 𝑀 𝑀 𝑗=1 log exp 𝑧𝑝𝑗 1,𝑎𝑗 (𝑦𝑗 ) 𝑣𝒱 exp 𝑧𝑝𝑗 1,𝑣 . (2) All other labels are ignored. Thus JSON punctuation, state tokens, and schema descriptions are context rather than supervised output targets. The objective is neither full-JSON generation loss nor full-token continued pretraining. The training path uses hard labels. 4 Intern-Decision: Efficient Multimodal Decision Model 3.4. Candidate probabilities and structured outputs At inference, only the legal candidate logits for each question are normalized: 𝑃𝑗(𝑐 𝑥; 𝑇 ) = exp(𝑧𝑝𝑗 1,𝑎𝑗 (𝑐)/𝑇 ) 𝑐𝒞𝑗 exp(𝑧𝑝𝑗 1,𝑎𝑗 (𝑐)/𝑇 ) , ˆ𝑦𝑗 = arg max 𝑐𝒞𝑗 𝑃𝑗(𝑐 𝑥; 𝑇 ). (3) positive scalar 𝑇 changes the probability spread without changing the argmax, apart from implementationlevel numerical ties. The serializer maps symbols back to original labels and creates the response object. Consequently, schema-conforming output does not depend on free-text decoder generating valid JSON. It also does not guarantee semantic correctness or agreement between related fields. The service can return the probability of yes for Boolean questions and an expected numeric value for ordinal questions. These quantities differ from the discrete argmax label used for decision accuracy. For all types, candidate probabilities and maximum probability remain available to downstream controllers. 3.5. Computational scope The method removes iterative answer decoding and avoids separate field-by-field forward passes. It does not eliminate the cost of processing the input: longer states, more image tokens, and larger schemas still increase computation and memory. One request may yield multiple decisions, so request rate and decision rate are different quantities. Causal ordering also means fields can have different contextual prefixes even when they share forward pass; the construction does not enforce permutation invariance or jointly constrained output distribution. 4. Data Construction 4.1. Decision-oriented data construction The decision corpus teaches structured choices rather than free-form answers. It combines synthetic textual decisions, public task distributions, and synthetic visual and interactive tasks. Each example contains visible state, optional images, typed questions, and target labels, allowing these sources to share the same decision interface. Table 1: Training dataset composition. Component Representative sources / tasks Capability focus Synthetic text decisions General and Hard decisions synthesized by deepseek-v4.1-flash Evidence use, rule following, and difficult textual judgments Public task distributions AG News [31], ToolACE [19], Typed Decisions [21], WildGuardMix [14], WildJailbreak [18], and Ruozhiba (LLM Ruozhiba QA and COIG-CQIA) [2, 15] Classification, tool routing, typed decisions, safety, and reasoning Synthetic visual and interactive tasks Game environments, VizDoom, and shapes/captcha-style tasks Visual grounding, discrete control, and pointer-action selection The released 0.8B, 2B, and 4B checkpoints use the same training input: 17,880 samples and 23,500 decisions, including 5,500 image-bearing samples. This identity is verified against input hashes, training logs, and tokenizer caches for all three runs. Figure 3 shows three components and nineteen categories, with the nine games listed individually. Sector areas encode samples, so multi-question record contributes once even when it supplies several supervised decisions. 5 Intern-Decision: Efficient Multimodal Decision Model The synthetic component uses text deepseek-v4.1-flash 1 as the teacher model. As Figure 3 shows, General contains 4,066 generalcategory synthetic decisions; Hard combines the hard and patch batches into 2,645 difficult-category synthetic decisions. We follow the Jevbench ability type to construct such general and hard synthetic decision examples. Public sources cover news classification, tool routing, typed decisions, and safety judgments. Synthetic visual sources supply rendered game frames, VizDoom observations, and shapes-based pointer actions. Appendix provides component counts, source descriptions, and representative records. The visual sources require recognition, comparison, target localization, and discrete action selection. Shapes tasks connect object attributes and spatial relations to pointer movements; game and VizDoom tasks connect frames to control decisions. These capabilities overlap within the recorded sources. Table 1 summarizes the evidenced source groups and their capability focus. 4.2. Calibration test set construction This evaluation-only test set measures whether the model assigns appropriate probabilities to all possible outcomes of stated random experiment. For example, fair die requires probability 1/6 on each real face and zero on impossible faces. Selecting one plausible face does not establish correct predictive distribution. Similarly, the Monty Hall questions ask where the prize is, with doors as outcomes; they do not ask whether switching is the best action. Figure 3: Training mixture shared by the released models. The inner ring shows components; numbered outer sectors show data categories, including each game. Counts are training-input samples. The set is constructed from 24 mechanism families in six categories. Each family has two settings, which vary numerical parameters or the observation protocol. Each setting is emitted with canonical and reversed option order, yielding 6 4 2 2 = 96 cases, 16 per category. The two order variants share the same state, question, and reference distribution. There are therefore 48 paired settings rather than 96 independent trials. Appendix gives the family inventory and concrete input/reference examples. For each setting, deterministic Python generator specifies the sample space, priors, independence assumptions, and observation or selection mechanism. It computes the exact distribution using rational arithmetic: counting and enumeration for finite outcomes, conditional-probability formulas for observed evidence, forward recursion for hidden states, and combinatorial or dynamic-programming calculations for sequential processes. References are not Monte Carlo estimates or model-generated answers. Construction checks enforce probabilities in [0, 1], an exact sum of one, matching option keys, unique IDs, and equivalent reversed-order pairs. Rebuilding from the archived generator reproduces the evaluated input and reference files byte for byte. Inputs contain only the state and typed questions. Exact fractions, numerical reference probabilities 𝑞𝑖, derivations, and provenance remain in separate reference file and are never sent to the model. The set is not used to train the model, fit its temperature, or select checkpoint. An exact-content check found no overlap 1https://huggingface.co/deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash 6 Intern-Decision: Efficient Multimodal Decision Model with the temperature-fitting records; this check does not establish absence of semantic overlap with every training source. In the actual three-door informed-host case, the prize is uniformly placed and the player initially selects door 1. host who knows the prize location always opens an unchosen empty door and always offers the other unopened door; legal reveals are chosen uniformly. The input does not disclose the opened doors number. The question is Where is the prize relative to the final two unopened doors? Its outcomes are initial_door and other_unopened_door, with reference probabilities 1/3 and 2/3. The initial selection retains its prior probability, and the hosts guaranteed safe reveal concentrates the other 2/3 on the remaining door. An output concentrated entirely on the remaining door would select the more likely outcome but misrepresent the residual uncertainty. 5. Evaluation Results 5.1. Decision accuracy Intern-Decision-4B has suite average of 90.02%, exceeding the baselines in Table 3, and leads or ties on five of the seven suites. It scores 1,611/2,000 (80.55%) on Typed Decision and 299/310 (96.45%) on ToolACE. On public Jevbench, it answers 48/48 Easy, 71/72 Original, and 82/111 Hard items correctly. Local inference latency Local measurements use one RTX 4090, BF16, SDPA, the native Hugging Face backend, Transformers 5.14.1, and flash-linear-attention 0.4.2. Each request has 289 input tokens and three fields: one choice, one Boolean, and one ordinal question. All three are answered in one forward pass with checkpoint-specific temperature scaling. This is fixed short-request measurement, not latency sweep over long contexts or screenshots. Figure 4: Jevbench-Hard reliability: 111 items and ten equal-width bins. Only populated bins are shown. These are derived request rates rather than measured saturated serving throughput. They do not imply the same frame rate for an interactive agent, which also incurs observation, image preprocessing, action execution, and environment-update costs. Batch size, warm-up, repetition count, timing boundaries, and Jev transport conditions are needed before interpreting the ratios as controlled hardware speedups. 5.4. Known-distribution calibration pilot The known-distribution calibration test set constructed in Section 4.2 contains 96 cases across six categories. It evaluates complete outcome distributions against exact reference probabilities. The question wording requests an outcome, while the native decision interface returns probability for every listed option. Intern-Decision maps the ordered options to legal answer tokens and applies the candidate softmax in Equation 3; Jev supplies its native API probability map. We score these complete distributions, rather than converting selected label into one-hot vector or counting how often repeated sampled answers occur. Normalization guarantees probability vector, but correctness must be measured against 𝑞𝑖. The final 4B checkpoint is evaluated with fixed XTuner backend and 𝑇 = 1.992418, fitted on separate calibration records. Jev uses version 1.13.0. Temperature scaling reduces overall expected Brier by 0.078 and expected ECE by 0.124 while preserving every argmax. Relative to Jev, it has lower Brier in five categories and lower ECE in five categories; it is worse on Brier for selective disclosure and on ECE for daily evidence. Overall ECE differs from the mean category ECE because the cases are rebinned together. For the informed-host three-door case described in Section 4.2, calibrated Intern-Decision returns (0.4222, 0.5778) and Jev returns (0.18, 0.82) in that order. Both select the more likely door, while their total variation distances from the reference are 0.0889 and 0.1533, respectively. The uncalibrated 4B distribution (0.3486, 0.6514) is closer still, so the overall gain from temperature scaling does not imply improvement on every case. Jev also returns separate confidence of 0.63 here, which is the value used by the pilot ECE protocol. Changing the observation mechanism changes the target: an uninformed host who randomly opens door, conditioned on revealing no prize, yields (1/2, 1/2). Appendix also explains selective-offer variant. 5.5. Confidence-based model handoff Let 𝑐(𝑥) be scalar confidence from the small model. simple cascade retains its answer when 𝑐(𝑥) 𝜏 and invokes larger model otherwise. The reported study routes 42 of the 111 public Hard items to Atria-DawnPreview [16], leaving 69 items with Intern-Decision-4B. The routed fraction is 37.84%, and local coverage is 62.16%. Table 7: Public model handoff study on Jevbench-Hard. The hybrid time is an estimate, while the Atria-only total is reported as measured. The local total is derived from 111 times the fixed-request mean latency and is not per-item Hard timing trace. System Correct / 111 Accuracy Atria calls Total time Intern-Decision-4B Confidence-based handoff Atria-Dawn-Preview only 82 97 99 73.87% 87.39% 89.19% 0 4.90 s, derived 42 140.16 s, estimated 111 300.03 s, measured The hybrid answers 15 more items correctly than the small model and two fewer than Atria alone. Relative to the reported Atria-only total, its estimated time is 53.29% lower. This illustrates potentially useful operating point rather than an established optimal policy. 6. Multimodal Interaction and Model Collaboration 6.1. closed-loop decision interface In an interactive controller, each iteration observes an environment state, forms candidate actions, evaluates them, executes the selected action, and observes the result. Intern-Decision supplies the local choice within this loop. The caller defines the action space and determines when to request another decision. The followIntern-Decision: Efficient Multimodal Decision Model ing demonstrations illustrate this interface; they are selected qualitative trajectories rather than controlled benchmark measurements. 6.2. Visual game control Five described demonstrations span Snake, fruit catching, Mario, and two first-person Doom tasks. They require different local decisions: selecting safe direction toward food, distinguishing fruit from hazards, coordinating movement and jumping, searching for health, or targeting an enemy. Screenshots provide visual evidence directly, so the controller can operate without converting every game state into symbolic text description. Figure 5: Qualitative examples of visual game control with Intern-Decision. From left to right: navigating toward food while avoiding the snake body; catching fruit while avoiding bombs; moving and jumping through Mario level; searching for health packs; and firing at approaching enemies. Each column shows two consecutive video frames, with the earlier frame on top and the later frame below. In the Doom health-gathering example, the agent changes its view after contacting wall and subsequently searches for new targets. This is an observed behavior in trajectory; it is not evidence of learned exploration objective or general exploration algorithm. Episode counts, seeds, returns, action frequency, observation history, and comparison policies are required for quantitative conclusions about game competence. The short text-request timing in Table 5 does not establish visual-control frame rate. 6.3. Visual selection and mouse actions CAPTCHA-style visual tasks require the integration of visual perception, instruction understanding, and interactive decision making. Intern-Decision directly observes interface screenshots, identifies targets described in natural language, and completes tasks through discrete mouse movements and clicks. The model must interpret object attributes and their relationships, translate visual judgments into executable actions, and use the updated screenshot after each action to guide the next decision, forming closed loop between perception and execution. 11 Intern-Decision: Efficient Multimodal Decision Model Figure 6: Visual selection trajectories rendered as static video strips. Each row contains five chronologically ordered frames: (a) selecting the largest red sphere; (b) selecting the smallest red cube; (c) identifying the odd shape; and (d) selecting the second blue object from the left. Arrows indicate temporal progression, with intermediate steps omitted. Panels preserve the recorded object layouts and cursor positions; interface text is translated into English for presentation, and video presentation overlays are omitted. Four demonstrations record successful trajectories in which Intern-Decision autonomously completes the tasks; Figure 6 presents selected keyframes in chronological order. Guided by the task instruction and the current screenshot, the model progressively moves the pointer, adjusts its position, and clicks the target without human takeover or correction. These examples illustrate the integration of multimodal understanding with sequential action selection and provide concrete experimental setting for studying visual interaction and task execution in graphical interfaces. 6.4. Hierarchical browser assistance We study browser use as hierarchical, closed-loop decision making rather than end-to-end free-form generation. Given natural-language goal, larger planner maintains cross-page context and proposes stage-level subgoal. At each iteration, the current page evidence and finite candidate set (e.g., click, scroll, return, or stop) are presented to Intern-Decision; the selected action is executed, and the page is observed again. The user task contains neither element identifiers nor scripted click sequence, so local actions are chosen from the live interface. 12 Intern-Decision: Efficient Multimodal Decision Model Figure 7: Browser-use trajectories rendered as static video strips. Each row contains five chronologically ordered frames: (a) Hugging Face checkpoint and configuration verification; (b) GitHub repository and API-reliability investigation; and (c) PyTorch documentation and pinned-source inspection. Arrows indicate temporal progression. All panels show the browser interface itself without the presentation overlays used in the demo videos. Figure 7 shows three selected trajectories on public websites. The Hugging Face task identifies the standard Atria-Dawn-Preview checkpoint and verifies both its configuration and default-reasoning template. The GitHub task starts from repository search, enters the official project, and locates an API-reliability issue reporting intermittent HTTP 422 and 502/503 responses. The PyTorch task verifies the evaluation-time dropout warning for scaled_dot_product_attention and follows the documented API to its pinned v2.14 implementation. The three traces reach the requested evidence in 6, 6, and 4 local decisions, respectively. Median Intern-Decision inference latency is 101.6, 109.8, and 95.3 ms (server-reported inference time, excluding planning, network, and browser execution). These examples are qualitative system demonstrations rather than browser benchmark. Dynamic pages can occasionally produce delayed or visually unchanged outcomes; the controller therefore re-observes the interface after every action and uses explicit completion checks to avoid unnecessary continuation. This division of labor lets the larger model handle goal decomposition and cross-page reasoning while Intern-Decision handles repeated, structured action selection. 7. Conclusion We introduce Intern-Decision, which makes finite multimodal choices through single causal forward pass, retaining the pretrained backbones native language-model head and exposing candidate probabilities through typed interface. The 4B model achieves the highest seven-suite average in the presented comparison, with 44.16 ms mean for fixed short request on an RTX 4090. Separate calibration and handoff studies show how probabilistic outputs can support uncertainty analysis and selective use of larger model. We believe Intern-Decision can serve as practical component of larger agent systems, but its generalization to arbitrarily large schemas and complex environments remains an open problem.

Release and Reproduction Details The public implementation documentation inspected for this draft is fixed to Git revision 2f815802058b. It identifies ordinary next-token alignment for the masked skeleton; historical same-position masked experiments are separate revisions. The published accuracy and pilot tables use XTuner, while the reported local latency uses native Hugging Face inference. checkpoint, tokenizer, processor, calibration artifact, and backend configuration together define an evaluated system. The released evaluation procedure consists of four stages. First, verify the bundled test hashes and counts. Second, bind the correct preset temperature to the exact checkpoint through metadata and weight-shard checks. Third, run uncalibrated inference and replay the fixed temperature on the saved probabilities, retaining complete raw outputs and verifying unchanged labels. Fourth, score the pilot separately using its exact references and require 96/96 valid outputs. External-baseline adapters and historical responses are not included, so reproducing Intern-Decision rows does not automatically reproduce every baseline row. Table 8: Full-precision released temperature presets. Each value belongs to its checkpoint and the reported XTuner execution setting; it is not freely transferable model-size constant.

sections.title: Mechanism coverage and reference construction
sections.content: The pilot consists of six categories with four families each. Every family has two settings and every setting has two option-order variants. The resulting 96 records cover the following mechanisms: 1. Direct randomness and support: uniform die faces with impossible options; weighted candy inventories; deterministic single-color pens; rare winning lottery tickets. 2. Composed events and mixtures: sums of two dice; numbers of independent hits; independent backup generators; delivery outcomes under an unobserved route mixture. 3. History, conditioning, and hidden state: independent coin flips after streak; socks after known removals; die outcomes given restricted sensor observation; two-state Markov process with noisy sensor readings. 4. Daily evidence and observation bias: defect screening with stated base rate; conditionally independent repeated tests; correlated copies of one test; waiting times observed at uniformly sampled time. 5. Selective disclosure and puzzles: informed-host Monty Hall; uninformed-host Monty Hall conditioned on safe reveal; prize-dependent switch offers; two-child problems with different child-selection protocols. 6. Sequential and combinatorial processes: distinct coupons collected after finite draws; birthday collisions on toy calendar; gamblers ruin; first-reward times with guaranteed stopping limit. The everyday descriptions define synthetic mechanisms with explicit parameters, not empirical frequencies inferred from real-world populations. Their oracles use exact rational arithmetic: finite counting, Bayes rule and total probability, hidden-state forward updates, coupon-count dynamic programming, birthday no-collision products, gamblers-ruin formulas, and truncated geometric probabilities. An input/reference pair carries stable ID and input hash. Validation verifies the option keys and probability support, exact normalization, and unchanged references when the option insertion order is reversed. Reference metadata records the family, setting, exact fractions, and derivation separately from the model-visible input. Support and conditioning: two further actual cases Fair die with impossible options. The state specifies fair six-faced die labeled 1 through 6, rolled once without landing on an edge or leaving the table. The question is What number will the die show? The ordered criteria contain labels 1, . . . , 8. The reference map is 𝑞 = {1 : 1/6, 2 : 1/6, 3 : 1/6, 4 : 1/6, 5 : 1/6, 6 : 1/6, 7 : 0, 8 : 0}. This tests equal mass across possible outcomes and zero mass on impossible ones. Returning one face with probability one fails the distribution test. Even perfect prediction has expected Brier 5/6, owing to outcome randomness, but zero excess expected Brier. Sampling after removal. The state says drawer initially contained six red and four blue socks; exactly three red socks were removed without replacement, with no other changes. One remaining sock is drawn uniformly. The question is What color is the selected sock? The reversed-order record lists blue then red; its exact reference is blue: 4/7, red: 3/7. The model must update the inventory before predicting the draw. Reversing criteria changes neither event probabilities nor the labels attached to them. Both cases use the same common random-experiment instruction shown in the Monty Hall input below. 19 Intern-Decision: Efficient Multimodal Decision Model Monty Hall: prize location as the outcome Here is an example of the three-door problem and models predictions. { "state": "A game has 3 doors and one prize, placed uniformly. You select door 1 before receiving any information. host who knows the prize location always opens exactly 1 unchosen doors that contain no prize, then always offers switch to the only other unopened door. If more than one legal reveal set exists, the host chooses uniformly among them. You observe this protocol being completed, but are not told which door numbers were opened.", "questions": { "decision": { "type": "choice", "instructions": "Where is the prize relative to the final two unopened doors? Predict the outcome of the specified random experiment using only its stated rules. The listed outcomes are mutually exclusive and exhaustive. Treat every stated probability, independence assumption, and observation protocol as exact.", "criteria": { "initial_door": "initial_door", "other_unopened_door": "other_unopened_door" } } } }
